story: Lesson 9 closes the rates section. With no table or diagram prompted, students choose a unit rate themselves to judge deals and compare distances. Percentages begin in Lesson 10.
previous: In Lesson 8 students used speed and pace to find unknown distances and times; today they pick which unit rate to find, then use it to decide.

clo.imGoal: Apply reasoning about ratios and rates to justify (orally) whether a given price is a good deal.
clo.form: Card ___ is (not) a good deal because the unit rate is ___ per ___ in the new deal and ___ per ___ in the original.
clo.statement: Students will justify orally whether a price is a good deal by comparing the unit rate in each offer, the price of one item, named with “per.”
clo.exemplar: Card A is a good deal because the unit rate is 75 cents per bottle in the new deal and 79 cents per bottle in the original.
clo.lookFor: The taco explanation names the better deal and gives the unit rate in each offer, with “per”: about $0.85 per taco (8.49 ÷ 10) against $0.90 per taco (5.40 ÷ 6).

posted.goal: We will say whether a price is a good deal and prove it with the unit rate: the price per item in each offer.
posted.sentence: 3 markers for $2.10 is a good deal because the unit rate is 70 cents per marker in the new deal and 80 cents per marker in the original.

strategies: A: see a 5 by 5 block, a quarter of the grid: \(\frac{25}{100}\), 0.25 or \(\frac{1}{4}\).
B: see one full column, a tenth: \(\frac{1}{10}\), \(\frac{10}{100}\) or 0.1.
C: see half the grid plus a quarter: \(\frac{75}{100}\), 0.75 or \(\frac{3}{4}\). Some may say 75%.
barriers: The whole grid stands for 1, not 100, which may be new.
The words “shaded portion” may be unfamiliar.
misconceptions: Counting every square, then naming the count, 25, instead of a part of 1.
Naming B as \(\frac{1}{100}\) because it is one column, not one square of ten.
backPocket: How did you see the shaded portion?
What is the whole grid worth?
Can you name it another way, as a decimal?
activities.grouping: Whole class: flash the image for 3 seconds, twice, with 15 seconds of quiet think time after each.
activities.monitor: Listen for ways of seeing (blocks, columns, halves) and for names in fractions, decimals and percents.

strategies: Compare both unit rates: card B is 35 cents per box before (3.50 ÷ 10) and 40 cents now (2.40 ÷ 6), so no deal.
Use the original unit rate on the new number: card A is 79 cents per bottle, so 3 bottles should cost $2.37; $2.25 is less, so deal.
Scale with no unit rate: 6 is \(\frac{6}{10}\) of 10, so 6 boxes should cost \(\frac{6}{10}\) of $3.50, $2.10; $2.40 is more, so no deal.
barriers: Dividing decimals, grade 5 work: 3.16 ÷ 4 may stop a pair who chose the right unit rate.
“Deal,” “original” and “new deal” on the cards: which price is which, and what makes a deal good.
misconceptions: “Deal, $2.25 is less than $3.16”: two totals for different numbers of bottles.
Finding 79 cents per bottle, then setting it against $2.25, the price of 3 bottles.
Language: “The new one is more,” with no “per” and no number of items.
backPocket: Less money, but for how many bottles?
Think in cents. How many cents is $3.16?
What should 3 bottles cost at the 4-pack price?
What does one box cost in each offer?
activities.grouping: Pairs: card A together, then two cards each, explained to the partner, then sorted together.
activities.monitor: Track which way each pair uses: unit rate, the original rate on the new number, or scaling the pack. Listen for “the same,” “unit rate,” “cost for the same number of items.”

strategies: Convert all to feet: antelope 5,280, cougar 4,224 (1,408 × 3), hare 4,136 (49,632 ÷ 12), coyote 3,773, ostrich about 3,772.97, kangaroo about 3,520.
Convert all to yards: antelope 1,760, cougar 1,408, hare \(1{,}378\frac{2}{3}\), and so on.
Convert all to meters using 1 inch = 2.54 centimeters: antelope about 1,609, ostrich 1,150, kangaroo 1,073. The order is the same: antelope, cougar, hare, coyote, ostrich, kangaroo.
barriers: Customary units (yards, feet, inches) may be unfamiliar next to metric ones.
1 inch = 2.54 centimeters is the only fact that links the two systems.
misconceptions: “The hare wins, 49,632 is the biggest number”: inches read against yards and meters.
Stopping at the kangaroo’s meters: there is no one meters-to-feet fact, so it takes several steps.
Calling the ostrich and coyote a tie: they differ by under half an inch.
backPocket: 49,632 what? What unit is the cougar’s in?
Which fact starts in meters? Where does it take you?
Which one unit would make comparing easiest?
activities.grouping: Alone: read for 1–2 minutes, agree as a class on units, convert in quiet think time, then share with students who chose the same unit.
activities.monitor: In the first 2–3 minutes, check who converts every distance to one unit. Note which unit each student picks, to group them for sharing.

m8: Asked what unit 49,632 is in instead of saying inches
Pointed to the cougar’s unit so they saw the units differ
Let them choose the one unit to convert to
m9: Asked which fact starts in meters instead of giving the chain
Pointed to 1 inch = 2.54 centimeters as the link
Let them work the steps: meters, centimeters, inches, feet

threeReads.say: Listen as I read card A. No numbers yet: what is happening?
threeReads.listenFor: A pack of drinks is missing a bottle, and the clerk offers a price for what’s left.

threeReads.say: Read it again. What does each number count, and in what unit?
threeReads.listenFor: 4 bottles for $3.16 in the full pack; 3 bottles for $2.25 now.

threeReads.say: Read it once more. How might we check if it’s a good deal?
threeReads.listenFor: Find the price of 1 bottle in each pack, find what 3 bottles should cost at the 4-pack price, or take \(\frac{3}{4}\) of $3.16.

release.successCriteria: Say deal or no deal, and compare fairly: the price per item, or the price of the same number of items.
release.say: Say deal or no deal. Then compare the two offers fairly: per item, or for the same number of items.
talkMoments: After card A, each partner says the card A reason aloud with the frame before you split the cards.
When partners explain their two cards, one uses the frame, and the other agrees or disagrees and says why.

emerging.frame: Card ___: deal / no deal, because ___ is less / more than ___.
emerging.stretch: They add “per”: “Deal, because 75 cents per bottle is less than 79 cents per bottle.”
emerging.nonverbal: Point to the two prices they compare, then thumbs up for deal or down for no deal.

developing.frame: Card ___ is a deal / no deal because ___ cost ___ now and ___ before.
developing.stretch: They name the rate: “The unit rate is 75 cents per bottle, not 79 cents per bottle.”
developing.nonverbal: Circle the two prices they compare, draw < or > between them, and point to the better offer.

expanding.frame: Card ___ is (not) a good deal because the unit rate is ___ per ___ in the new deal and ___ per ___ in the original.
expanding.stretch: They check another way: “At the old price 3 bottles cost $2.37, and $2.25 is less.”
expanding.nonverbal: Write the two prices they compare side by side with < or >, then place the card on its pile.

steps: During partner talk, scribe students’ words as said, such as “the same” or “cost for the same number of items,” and write the precise term (“unit rate,” “per”) beside them.
Call 2–3 pairs: unit rate first, then the original rate on the new number, then scaling the pack.
Scribe each pair’s reason as said beside its numbers; add “unit rate” or “per” next to their words, not in place of them.
Ask pairs to compare the ways. Which used a unit rate? How does scaling the pack reach the same decision? Students make the connections; you scribe them.
Leave the display up for the lesson synthesis and the cool-down.
synthesis.prompt: Is card B a good deal? How do you know?
synthesis.sounds: Card B is not a good deal because the unit rate is 40 cents per box in the new deal and 35 cents per box in the original.

rehearsal.student: A student stops at the kangaroo: “There’s no meters to feet.”
rehearsal.ask: What do you say to this student?
rehearsal.aim: The student builds the chain from meters to feet, one fact at a time.
say: Which fact starts in meters? Where does it take you?
checks: Asked which fact starts in meters instead of giving the chain
Pointed to 1 inch = 2.54 centimeters as the link
Let them work the steps: meters, centimeters, inches, feet
rehearsal.ifNot: How many centimeters are in 1 meter?
rehearsal.goingOn: The student converted four of six distances to feet correctly. The kangaroo needs a chain of facts, since no single fact goes from meters to feet.

ideas: To compare two rates, compare unit rates: the price of one item in each offer.
10 juice boxes for $3.50 is $0.35 per box, because 3.50 ÷ 10 = 0.35. 6 for $2.40 is $0.40 per box, because 2.40 ÷ 6 = 0.40.
Each is a unit rate, $0.35 per box against $0.40 per box, so the 10-pack is the better deal.
lessonSynthesis.pointTo: Point to the 9.2 display: card B’s $0.35 and $0.40 per box, and the words beside them. If you taught 9.3, point to its rankings: one unit before comparing.

check.question: Stickers cost 4 for $1.00, or 10 for $2.00. Which offer is the better deal, and why?
check.sounds: 10 for $2.00 is the better deal because the unit rate is 20 cents per sticker there and 25 cents per sticker in the other offer.

cuts.note: Keep it short: two flashes, one way of seeing each grid.
Protect quiet think time; it meets IM’s first goal. Keep the ranking, and hear two students: one in feet or yards, one in meters. Lost: why both orders match.
Leave out card F (IM’s extension) unless pairs finish early. Keep Three Reads quick, one sentence each. Never cut the card A reason, partners explaining their cards, or the synthesis.
